findings.title: SQL built by string interpolation and passed to pool.query()

evidence.excerpt: const sql = `SELECT * FROM "Product" WHERE name LIKE '%${term}%'`;
evidence.note: untrusted value interpolated into query text
the built string is passed to pool.query()

steps.detail: query text assembled with interpolation
passed to pool.query() as statement text

findings.explanation: The statement passed to pool.query() is assembled by interpolation rather than parameterised. Any value reaching that interpolation is executed as SQL, not treated as data.
findings.userImpact: An attacker who controls the interpolated value can read, modify, or delete any data the database user can reach, including other customers' records, and in many configurations can escalate further.
findings.likelyRootCause: A query was written as a string because the value was assumed to be internal or already validated.
downstreamConsequences: Input validation elsewhere does not fix this: the vulnerability is in how the statement is built.
Database audit logs will show the injected statement as a legitimate application query.
findings.remediation: Replace the interpolation with a parameterised query: pass values as bind parameters ($1/? placeholders or the ORM's tagged-template form such as Prisma's `$queryRaw` with template parameters) so the driver sends them separately from the statement text. Where an identifier (table or column name) genuinely must be dynamic, validate it against a fixed allowlist.
verificationSteps: Confirm the query now passes values as bind parameters.
Add a regression test that supplies a value containing a quote and a semicolon and asserts it is stored or matched literally.
Confirm no remaining call site builds this statement by concatenation.
references: OWASP A03:2021 Injection
CWE-89 SQL Injection
findings.priorityRationale: P0: critical severity with confirmed confidence, security-relevant, touches many components, low remediation effort. Confirmed and consequential enough to block release.

findings.title: DELETE /api/orders/[id] performs no authentication check

evidence.excerpt: export async function DELETE(req: Request, { params }: { params: { id: string } }) {
evidence.note: handler DELETE contains no authentication check

steps.detail: DELETE /api/orders/[id] handler declared

handler queries the Order model

findings.explanation: The handler for DELETE /api/orders/[id] does not call any session or authentication helper, and no rejection path for an unauthenticated caller exists in its body. It queries: Order.
findings.userImpact: An unauthenticated caller can change or destroy stored data.
findings.likelyRootCause: The route was added without the project's authentication helper, or enforcement was assumed to be global.

Rate limiting and logging will record the access as anonymous traffic.

Enforce this server-side in the handler (or in middleware that provably matches this path), not in the client.
verificationSteps: Call DELETE /api/orders/[id] with no credentials and confirm a 401.
Call it with a valid session and confirm the previous behaviour is unchanged.
Confirm a caller cannot read another account's data.

findings.title: GET /api/orders/[id] reads a Order by request id without checking ownership

evidence.excerpt: export async function GET(req: Request, { params }: { params: { id: string } }) {
evidence.note: session is resolved, so the caller is authenticated
Order looked up by an identifier taken from the request (id)
the model has an ownership column 'userId' that this query does not filter on

steps.detail: authentication enforced: an unauthenticated caller is rejected
prisma.order.findUnique() keyed by request value 'id'
Order.userId identifies the owning user
no comparison between userId and the session identity anywhere in the handler

findings.explanation: The handler authenticates the caller but then loads a Order using the 'id' value from the request, without restricting the query to records the caller owns. Order has an ownership column ('userId'), and it is never compared with the session identity in this handler. Authentication answers "who is this"; this handler never answers "may they see this record".
findings.userImpact: Any logged-in user can read or modify another user's Order records simply by changing the identifier in the URL. This is the most commonly exploited class of API flaw and requires no special tooling.
findings.likelyRootCause: The authentication check was added and mistaken for an authorisation check, which is a very common conflation.
downstreamConsequences: Every other handler that loads a Order by request id likely has the same gap.
Sequential or guessable identifiers make enumeration trivial; opaque ids reduce but do not remove the exposure.
findings.remediation: Scope the query to the caller: include 'userId' from the resolved session in the where clause (for example `where: { id, userId: session.userId }`) so a record belonging to someone else simply is not found. Where administrators must bypass this, branch on an explicit role check rather than widening the default query. Returning 404 rather than 403 for a record the caller does not own avoids confirming that it exists.
verificationSteps: Create records for two different users, then request user A's Order while authenticated as user B and confirm it is not returned.
Confirm the owner can still read and modify their own records.
Add a regression test covering all three cases: unauthenticated, owner, and non-owner.
Audit the other handlers that load this model by request id.
references: OWASP A01:2021 Broken Access Control
CWE-639 Authorization Bypass Through User-Controlled Key
OWASP API Security Top 10: API1 Broken Object Level Authorization
findings.priorityRationale: P0: critical severity with strong confidence, security-relevant, touches many components, low remediation effort, must wait for 1 prerequisite fix(es). Confirmed and consequential enough to block release.

findings.title: Environment file with live-looking credentials is committed: .env

evidence.excerpt: 4 credential-shaped value(s): DATABASE_URL (database connection string with password), STRIPE_SECRET_KEY (hardcoded value assigned to 'STRIPE_SECRET_KEY'), JWT_SECRET (hardcoded value assigned to 'JWT_SECRET'), OPENAI_API_KEY (hardcoded value assigned to 'OPENAI_API_KEY')

findings.explanation: .env is tracked in the repository and contains 4 value(s) matching live credential shapes. An environment file is meant to hold deployment configuration and stay out of version control.

Confirm the application reads each value from the deployment environment.
Confirm each old credential is revoked at its provider.

findings.title: POST /api/webhooks/stripe processes webhook payloads without verifying the signature

evidence.note: the signature header is read but never passed to a verification function

findings.explanation: The handler acts on the request body without verifying that it came from the provider. The signature header is read, which suggests verification was intended, but the value is never checked against the signing secret. A webhook URL is effectively public: it must be assumed that attackers know it.
findings.userImpact: Anyone can forge a request to this endpoint and cause whatever the handler does — marking orders paid, granting entitlements, or changing account state — without any real payment or provider event.
findings.likelyRootCause: Verification is commonly skipped during local development and then not added before release.
downstreamConsequences: Financial state can be changed by an unauthenticated caller.
Provider-side event logs will not show the forged events, making reconciliation misleading.
findings.remediation: Verify every delivery before acting on it: read the raw request body (not the parsed JSON, since re-serialising changes the bytes), compute or verify the HMAC against the provider signing secret with a constant-time compare — or use the provider SDK's own verification helper, such as Stripe's `constructEvent` — reject with 400 on failure, and enforce the provider's timestamp tolerance to prevent replay.
verificationSteps: Send a payload with no signature and confirm it is rejected.
Send a payload with a wrong signature and confirm it is rejected.
Send a correctly signed payload and confirm it is processed exactly once.
Confirm the handler reads the raw body, since parsing before verification breaks the HMAC.
references: OWASP A08:2021 Software and Data Integrity Failures
CWE-345 Insufficient Verification of Data Authenticity

findings.title: POST /api/login compares passwords without hashing

evidence.note: stored value compared directly against the submitted password; no hashing function is used in this handler

findings.explanation: The handler compares a stored password value directly with the submitted one. No password hashing function (bcrypt, argon2, scrypt, or PBKDF2) appears in this handler, which means the stored value is the password itself. The comparison is also not constant-time, so it leaks information through timing.
findings.userImpact: If the database is ever read by an attacker — through a backup, a log, an injection flaw, or an insider — every user's password is immediately usable, including on the other services where people reuse passwords.
findings.likelyRootCause: Authentication was built against a plaintext column during early development and never migrated.
downstreamConsequences: Migration requires a rehash-on-next-login path; existing stored values cannot be recovered into hashes.
Password reuse means the breach extends beyond this application.
findings.remediation: Store a hash produced by argon2id, scrypt, or bcrypt with a per-user salt, and verify with that library's constant-time compare. Migrate by adding a hash column, hashing on next successful login, and removing the plaintext column once no rows depend on it. Treat all existing passwords as compromised and require a reset.
verificationSteps: Confirm the stored column holds a hash with a recognisable algorithm prefix.
Confirm login succeeds for a newly set password and fails for a wrong one.
Confirm no code path reads or logs the plaintext password.
references: OWASP A02:2021 Cryptographic Failures
CWE-256 Plaintext Storage of a Password

findings.title: POST /api/webhooks/stripe marks the record settled before reading the payment outcome

evidence.note: the record is marked settled here, unconditionally
the provider's outcome is only examined here, after the write above

steps.detail: prisma.order.update sets the settled state with no condition on the outcome
the success/failure branch is evaluated after the state has already been written

findings.explanation: In the POST /api/webhooks/stripe handler the record is marked settled at line 19, and the provider's outcome field is not examined until line 24. The write is therefore unconditional: it runs for a failed charge, a cancelled payment, a dispute, and a test event exactly as it runs for a successful one. The branch below can log the failure or alert on it, but the state it would need to prevent has already been committed, and nothing in this handler reverses it.
findings.userImpact: An order whose payment failed is treated as paid: it is fulfilled, shipped, or unlocked, and the customer receives goods or access that was never paid for. The mirror case is just as bad — a customer whose payment genuinely succeeded cannot be distinguished from one whose did not, so support has no reliable answer, and the business discovers the gap through reconciliation rather than through the application.
findings.likelyRootCause: The handler was written for the success event and later extended with a failure branch, which was appended to the end of the function instead of placed before the state change.
downstreamConsequences: Revenue reported by the application diverges from the provider's settlement records.
Fulfilment, entitlement, and email flows triggered by the settled state all fire on failed payments.
Correcting the data later requires matching every affected record against the provider by hand.
findings.remediation: Read the outcome first and make the state change conditional on it. Branch on the event type or the payment status at the top of the handler, return early for anything that is not a confirmed success, and only then write the settled state — ideally in the same transaction as the idempotency record, so a crash cannot settle a record without logging why. Treat unknown or new event types as "do nothing" rather than as success, and let the provider retry what you did not handle.
verificationSteps: Send a failure event (the provider's test mode can generate a declined charge) and confirm the record is not marked settled.
Send a success event and confirm it is.
Send an event type the handler does not recognise and confirm nothing changes.
Query for records in the settled state whose provider payment is not successful, to size any damage already done.
references: CWE-840 Business Logic Errors
CWE-696 Incorrect Behavior Order
findings.priorityRationale: P0: critical severity with strong confidence, direct user-visible impact, low remediation effort. Confirmed and consequential enough to block release.

findings.title: PUT /api/upload fetches a URL supplied in the request

evidence.note: the destination URL comes from request input and is fetched without validation

steps.detail: PUT /api/upload reads a URL from the request
fetch() is called with that value

findings.explanation: The handler issues a server-side request to a URL taken from the request body or query. The server can usually reach addresses the caller cannot: cloud instance metadata endpoints, internal services, and localhost-bound admin interfaces.
findings.userImpact: An attacker can make the server fetch internal addresses and return the response to them — on many cloud providers that includes the instance metadata service and therefore credentials. It also turns the server into a proxy for scanning the internal network.
findings.likelyRootCause: A feature that legitimately needs to fetch a remote resource was implemented without constraining where it may point.
downstreamConsequences: A blocklist of IP literals is not sufficient: DNS names, redirects, and alternative encodings bypass it.
Returning the response body to the caller turns the flaw into a direct read of internal services.
findings.remediation: Constrain the destination: require https, resolve the hostname and reject private, loopback, link-local, and metadata ranges (checking after DNS resolution, and again on every redirect), prefer an allowlist of permitted hosts, disable redirect following or re-validate each hop, set a timeout and response size cap, and do not return the raw upstream body to the caller. Where possible route such requests through an egress proxy that enforces these rules centrally.
verificationSteps: Request `http://127.0.0.1/` and confirm it is rejected.
Request `http://169.254.169.254/` and confirm it is rejected.
Request a URL that redirects to a private address and confirm the redirect is rejected.
Confirm legitimate allowed destinations still work.
references: OWASP A10:2021 Server-Side Request Forgery
CWE-918 Server-Side Request Forgery

evidence.excerpt: // DEFECT (plaintext credential storage): no hash column, password stored raw.
evidence.note: column holds a credential and no password hashing library was found anywhere in the project

findings.title: POST /api/login accepts unlimited authentication attempts

evidence.note: authentication handler with no rate limiting in its body, and no rate-limiting dependency anywhere in the project

findings.explanation: The POST /api/login handler performs no rate limiting, and no rate-limiting library or middleware was found in the project. Credential guessing is therefore bounded only by network throughput.
findings.userImpact: Attackers can brute-force passwords and run credential-stuffing attacks against the login endpoint, compromising accounts whose passwords are weak or reused. Users may also be locked out or the service degraded by the attempt volume.
findings.likelyRootCause: Rate limiting is often deferred to infrastructure and then never configured.
downstreamConsequences: Password strength rules alone do not stop credential stuffing with breached passwords.
Without limits there is no natural signal that an attack is in progress.
findings.remediation: Apply a rate limit keyed on both client IP and the submitted account identifier, with exponential backoff or a temporary lockout after repeated failures. Enforce it server-side ahead of the credential check, log the rejections, and return a uniform error so the limiter does not itself leak which accounts exist.
verificationSteps: Send repeated failed attempts for one account and confirm later attempts are rejected.
Confirm a legitimate user is not blocked by normal use.
Confirm rejected attempts appear in the logs.
references: OWASP A07:2021 Identification and Authentication Failures
CWE-307 Improper Restriction of Excessive Authentication Attempts

findings.title: POST /api/upload accepts uploads unsafely (3 issues)

evidence.note: no content-type or extension allowlist; no size limit; the client-supplied filename is used to build the destination path

findings.explanation: The upload handler has the following gaps: no content-type or extension allowlist; no size limit; the client-supplied filename is used to build the destination path. Because the destination path is built from the client-supplied filename, a name containing path separators or `..` writes outside the intended directory. Without a type allowlist, content that the web server will execute or that browsers will treat as active content can be stored and then served.
findings.userImpact: An attacker can write a file to an arbitrary location the process can reach, which can overwrite application files or place executable content inside the served directory.
findings.likelyRootCause: Upload handling was written for the happy path with a trusted browser form in mind.
downstreamConsequences: Files stored now may already be hostile; existing contents need review, not just a code fix.
A CDN or static route may serve stored files with a content type that makes them active.
findings.remediation: Generate the stored filename server-side (a UUID plus an extension derived from a verified type) and never use the client-supplied name in a path. Enforce an explicit content-type allowlist validated against the file's actual bytes rather than the declared header, cap the size before buffering the whole file, store uploads outside the web root or in object storage, and serve them with `Content-Disposition: attachment` and a restrictive content type.
verificationSteps: Upload a file named `../../evil.txt` and confirm it lands inside the upload directory under a generated name.
Upload a disallowed type and confirm rejection.
Upload a file over the limit and confirm it is rejected before being fully buffered.
references: OWASP A04:2021 Insecure Design
CWE-434 Unrestricted Upload of File with Dangerous Type
CWE-22 Path Traversal
findings.priorityRationale: P1: high severity with strong confidence, security-relevant.

findings.title: Unsanitised value rendered as HTML in <div>

evidence.note: dangerouslySetInnerHTML receives a dynamic value with no sanitisation in this expression

findings.explanation: A dynamic value is passed to dangerouslySetInnerHTML on <div>, which bypasses React's automatic escaping. If any part of that value originates from user input or from stored data that a user can influence, the markup it contains executes in the browser of whoever views the page.
findings.userImpact: A visitor viewing this content can have script run in their session: their token can be stolen, actions can be performed as them, or the page can be rewritten to phish them. Stored content makes it persistent, affecting every viewer.
findings.likelyRootCause: Rich text or markdown needed to render as HTML and the value was passed through unsanitised.
downstreamConsequences: A Content-Security-Policy reduces but does not eliminate the impact.
Already-stored values may contain payloads: existing data needs review as well as the code fix.
findings.remediation: Render the value as text if it does not need to be HTML. If it must be HTML, sanitise it with a maintained sanitiser (DOMPurify or equivalent) using a strict allowlist of tags and attributes — ideally on write, server-side, so stored data is clean — and add a Content-Security-Policy that forbids inline script as defence in depth.
verificationSteps: Store a value containing ``, render the page, and confirm no script executes.
Confirm legitimate formatting still renders.
Confirm existing stored rows have been sanitised.
references: OWASP A03:2021 Injection
CWE-79 Cross-site Scripting

findings.title: OrderSummary.tsx reads customerName, which GET /api/orders/[id] never sends

evidence.note: the frontend reads order.customerName from the response of GET /api/orders/[id]
OrderView declares customerName as a non-optional member of that response

evidence.excerpt: return NextResponse.json({ id: order.id, total: order.total, items: order.items });
evidence.note: the handler responds with { error, id, total, items } — customerName is not among the keys
client call that fetches GET /api/orders/[id]

steps.detail: declares the response as { id, total, customerName, shippedAt, items }
calls GET /api/orders/[id]
reads order.customerName from the parsed response
handler returns { error, id, total, items }, without customerName

findings.explanation: src/components/OrderSummary.tsx declares the response of GET /api/orders/[id] as OrderView, which includes a required member `customerName`, and reads `order.customerName` at line 31. The handler in src/app/api/orders/[id]/route.ts responds with an object literal whose keys are { error, id, total, items }. `customerName` is never serialised, so at runtime the property is `undefined` — the declared type says otherwise, and because the type is a compile-time assertion about data that crosses a network boundary, the compiler cannot catch the disagreement. No single file shows this: the declaration and the read are in the component, the omission is in the handler.
findings.userImpact: Wherever customerName is shown, the user sees an empty space, the literal text "undefined", or a blank field, depending on how it is rendered. Nothing fails loudly: the page renders, the request succeeds, and the information the user came for is simply absent. If the value feeds a calculation or a comparison instead of being displayed, the result is wrong rather than missing.
findings.likelyRootCause: The response type was written from the intended shape of the feature, or copied from the data model, rather than from what the handler actually returns — or the handler was later narrowed and the consumer was not updated.
downstreamConsequences: Every other consumer of OrderView inherits the same wrong assumption.
TypeScript reports no error, so the build and the type-check both pass.
Adding customerName to the handler is a response-shape change, and any client caching the old shape must be considered.
findings.remediation: Decide which end is correct. If the field belongs in the response, add it to the handler's returned object and make sure the query actually selects it. If it does not, remove it from OrderView and from the render path, and let the compiler point at every consumer. To stop the pair drifting again, derive one end from the other: generate the client type from the handler (or from a shared schema validated at the boundary) instead of declaring it twice by hand, and parse the response against that schema so a missing field fails at the boundary rather than silently rendering as undefined.
verificationSteps: Call GET /api/orders/[id] directly and inspect the JSON body for a `customerName` key.
Render the component against that real response and confirm customerName displays a value.
Add a test that asserts the handler's response contains every required member of OrderView.
references: CWE-1288 Improper Validation of Consistency within Input
OpenAPI / typed-contract generation as the standard remedy for duplicated response types
findings.priorityRationale: P1: high severity with strong confidence, direct user-visible impact, low remediation effort.

findings.explanation: Webhook providers guarantee at-least-once delivery, not exactly-once: a delivery is retried whenever the response is slow, non-2xx, or lost, and the same event id arrives again. The duplicate insert therefore succeeds, and every state change in the handler (prisma.order.update) runs a second time. Neither file shows the problem alone: the handler looks like it is recording events, and the schema looks like an ordinary table.
findings.userImpact: A customer can be charged, credited, or fulfilled twice for one real event — the duplicate looks exactly like a legitimate second event, so it is not caught until someone reconciles the books or the customer complains. findings.likelyRootCause: The handler was written against a single successful delivery. Retries only appear in production, under exactly the conditions (timeouts, deploys, provider incidents) that make them hardest to notice.
downstreamConsequences: Retries cluster during incidents and deploys, so duplicates arrive precisely when the team is already busy.

Run the insert and the state change in one transaction so a crash between them cannot leave the event recorded but the work undone. findings.explanation: Dockerfile copies the entire build context with `COPY . .`, and .env is tracked in the repository, so the file becomes part of the image. No .dockerignore exists, so nothing is excluded from the build context. An image layer is not private storage: anyone who can pull the image can extract the file with `docker save`, and the layer persists in the registry and in the build cache even if a later instruction deletes the file. This is distinct from the file being committed at all — that is a source-control problem; this is the image distributing it to every host, CI job, and registry mirror that ever receives a pull.

Text appearing later in the same message does not constrain text that appeared earlier: an input ending with "ignore the preceding instructions and ..." sits at the same privilege level as the rules around it, and there is no delimiter or hierarchy statement separating the two. If the model's reply is then trusted by downstream code, the override reaches those code paths too.

Put the instructions in the system message with no interpolation of request values, and pass the untrusted text as a separate role:'user' message (or, for retrieved documents, as clearly labelled context in a user-role message). Confirm the system message in the outgoing request body is byte-identical for two different user inputs.
Add a regression test asserting the system message contains no request-derived substring.

findings.title: Database query inside a for loop (N+1 against Order)

evidence.excerpt: const orders = await prisma.order.findMany({ where: { userId: user.id } });
evidence.note: prisma.order.findMany() sits inside a for loop, so it runs once per element

evidence.excerpt: const users = await prisma.user.findMany({ include: { orders: true } });
evidence.note: an earlier query in the same handler already fetched 'orders' for every row

findings.explanation: prisma.order.findMany() is issued inside a for loop, so the number of database round trips is 1 for the outer collection plus one more for every element it contains — 1 + N, where N is the size of that collection at run time. N is not known statically and this scan does not measure it, so no multiplier is stated here; what is certain from the syntax tree is that the count scales with the data rather than staying fixed. Because the call is awaited inside the loop, each round trip also waits for the previous one to finish, so the waiting accumulates on top of the query count. The collection being iterated is itself the result of a query with no row ceiling, so N here is the size of a table rather than a fixed batch. The same handler already loaded 'orders' through an include on an earlier query, so this loop re-fetches rows the process is already holding in memory.
findings.userImpact: As the underlying collection grows, the page or endpoint takes progressively longer to respond and occupies a database connection throughout. Behaviour looks correct with a handful of seeded rows and degrades or times out at production volume, typically for the accounts with the most data — the heaviest users are hit first.
findings.likelyRootCause: The relation was added to an include for one purpose, and a later change fetched it again per row rather than reading the already-loaded field.
downstreamConsequences: Connection-pool pressure: one slow request of this shape can hold a connection long enough to starve other requests.
The cost is invisible in local testing, because it is proportional to the row count, not to the code path.
Any further handler that loops over the same collection almost certainly repeats the pattern.

Where the included relation is not enough, replace the loop with a single query: fetch all the rows you need in one call filtered by an `in` list of the parent identifiers, or use the ORM's aggregation (for example a grouped count) so the database does the per-parent work. If the relation is only needed for a count, select the count rather than the rows.
verificationSteps: Enable the ORM or database query log for one request to this code path and confirm the number of statements no longer grows with the number of rows returned by the outer query.
Seed the outer collection with a realistically large number of rows in a scratch database and compare the statement count before and after the change.
Add a regression test that asserts the statement count for GET /api/admin/stats is constant with respect to the row count.

imports searchProductsRaw, so requests served by this module queue on the same pool

steps.detail: Pool constructed once at module scope with no size option
pool.query() draws a connection from that pool
imports searchProductsRaw from the pool module, so this request path shares the pool
that consumer is reachable from an HTTP route, so the one pool is shared across concurrent requests

findings.explanation: The pool is constructed once per process at src/lib/db.ts:5 and no size option (`max`, `connectionLimit`, `poolSize`, `connection_limit` or the driver's equivalent) is set, so the number of connections this process will hold is whatever the driver defaults to. Two things follow. First, the limit is implicit: nobody reading this code can see what it is, and it changes if the driver is upgraded. Second, it is a per-process limit, while the constraint that actually matters is the database server's own maximum connection count, shared by every instance of this application plus migrations and any admin tooling. Nothing in the source connects the two numbers, so adding instances to absorb load silently multiplies the demand on the database. No concurrency figure is stated here deliberately: the point at which this becomes material depends on the database configuration and the real request mix, and neither is visible in a source snapshot.
findings.userImpact: Once every connection in the pool is busy, further requests do not fail — they wait for one to be released. Users see pages that touch the database get slower and then time out, while health checks that do not touch the database keep reporting the application as healthy. If instances are added, the database can begin refusing connections outright, which appears to users as errors scattered across unrelated parts of the application at the same time.
findings.likelyRootCause: The pool was created with the minimum options needed to connect during development, where one process and a handful of concurrent requests never reach the default ceiling.
downstreamConsequences: A saturated pool with no acquisition timeout turns a slow query into a queue that every request joins, which is how one slow endpoint takes down unrelated ones.
Serverless or autoscaled deployments create a new pool per instance, so the total connection demand tracks instance count rather than anything configured here.
Because the limit is implicit, a driver upgrade can change the application's capacity profile with no code change.
findings.remediation: Set the pool size explicitly where the pool is constructed, and derive the value rather than picking it: divide the database's configured maximum connections by the maximum number of application instances you will run (including the overlap during a rolling deploy), and leave headroom for migrations and administrative sessions. Set an acquisition timeout as well (`connectionTimeoutMillis` or the driver's equivalent) so a saturated pool fails fast with a clear error instead of queueing indefinitely, and an idle timeout so idle instances release connections. Where the instance count is elastic, put an external pooler in front of the database so the application's pool size no longer has to be coordinated by hand. Record the chosen numbers and their derivation next to the construction site.
verificationSteps: Read the database's configured connection maximum (on PostgreSQL, `SHOW max_connections`) and the per-user limit, then write down pool size × maximum instance count including deploy overlap and confirm the total fits with headroom.

Set the bound explicitly, then run a load test at the concurrency you intend to support and watch connection-acquisition wait time: this is the only way to size the pool, and it cannot be derived from the source.
With the pool deliberately saturated, confirm that a request fails with a clear acquisition timeout rather than hanging, and that the readiness probe reflects it.
Confirm the number of established connections per instance against the database's own connection view (for example `pg_stat_activity`) during that load test.

findings.title: prisma.product.findMany() reads every row and every column of Product

evidence.note: read with no filter, no row ceiling, and no column projection: every row and every column of the table
Product declares 4 columns; all of them are transferred by this query

steps.detail: prisma.product.findMany() called with no filter, ceiling, or projection
Product has 4 declared columns, so each returned row carries all of them
6 modules import this module, so the read is reachable from those callers

findings.explanation: prisma.product.findMany() places no bound of any kind on what it retrieves: no filter to narrow the rows, no take/limit to cap them, and no column selection to narrow each row. Every Product row and all 4 of its columns are read, transferred, and deserialised on every call. The billed quantities here are database read units and I/O, data transfer out of the database, and the application memory needed to hold the result. All three scale with the table, and the table size is a property of the deployment that this scan cannot see — so no figure is given.
findings.userImpact: The feature behind this read is fast on a small table and gets steadily slower and more memory-hungry as the table fills, until it times out. Because the cost is shared — the same database, the same process memory — the slowdown is felt by users of other features too, not only this one.
findings.likelyRootCause: The helper was written when the table was known to be small, so no bound was needed; the bound was never added as the data grew.
downstreamConsequences: Cost grows with the table rather than with usage, so it rises even while traffic is flat.
Adding a column to the model silently increases the cost of every call to this helper.
Most managed databases bill data transfer, so rows the caller never inspects are still paid for.
findings.remediation: Give the query a ceiling and a projection: select only the columns the callers read, and add an explicit row limit with paging (a limit with a sane default and a hard maximum, plus a cursor) so the per-call cost is set by the code. Because this is an exported helper, change the signature to require the bound rather than defaulting to unbounded, so a new caller cannot reintroduce the whole-table read. Where a whole-table pass is genuinely required (an export, a migration), stream it in cursor-based batches so memory stays flat, and run it off the request path.
verificationSteps: Seed the table to a realistically large row count and confirm the returned row count is capped by the query rather than by the data.
Record the rows read and bytes returned for this query from the database's own statistics before and after the change — that is the measurement that quantifies the saving.
Confirm every caller still receives the fields it uses after the projection is narrowed.

Data minimisation: fetch only the fields the caller needs

steps.detail: client.chat.completions.create() produces free-form text

findings.explanation: The handler for POST /api/chat returns the model's text to the caller exactly as received. There is no structured-output mode on the request, no schema parse of the result, no length bound, and no check of what the text contains. The response shape the client depends on is therefore whatever the model produced for that request: a model or prompt change, a refusal, a truncated generation, or an empty completion all arrive at the client as a successful 200.

Because the response still carries a success status, the UI has nothing to branch on and shows the broken result rather than an error state.
findings.likelyRootCause: The happy path was built first and the model returned sensible text during development, so the parse step never looked necessary.
downstreamConsequences: If the client renders this text as markup rather than text, unvalidated output becomes a rendering and script-injection path as well.
Without a validation step there is no place to attach the retry that a malformed generation needs.
findings.remediation: Ask the provider for structured output (a JSON schema or the SDK's object-generation call) and parse the result against that schema server-side before responding — a typed schema library makes the parse the single place the shape is enforced. On a parse failure, retry once and then return an explicit error status rather than passing the text through. Bound the length, and keep the client rendering the value as text unless it has been sanitised for markup.
verificationSteps: Point the handler at a stub that returns an empty string and confirm the endpoint returns an error rather than a 200 with empty content.
Point it at a stub returning text that violates the expected shape and confirm the parse rejects it.
Confirm the normal path still returns the expected shape, and add a regression test for all three.

When that I/O fails, and it will (a dropped connection, a constraint violation, a timeout, a provider incident), the rejection propagates out of the handler. The framework turns it into a generic 500 with no application-specific body, no structured log line identifying which operation failed, and no partial cleanup of anything the handler had already changed.

Because the response cannot distinguish those cases, the interface cannot tell the user whether to fix their input, retry, or wait, so the usual outcome is an abandoned task and a support request. For a write that partly completed, the user is left not knowing what state their data is in.

downstreamConsequences: Failures are indistinguishable in the logs, so the first step of every investigation is reproducing the request.
A write that fails halfway leaves the record in an intermediate state that no later code expects.
Error-rate metrics cannot separate client mistakes from dependency failures.

In the catch: log with enough context to identify the operation and the record, map known failures onto honest status codes (400 for bad input, 404 for missing, 409 for a conflict, 503 for an unavailable dependency), and return a body the interface can act on. findings.title: POST /api/webhooks/stripe applies several writes with no transaction on an at-least-once delivery path

evidence.note: first persisted write (prisma.order.update), applied before anything establishes that this delivery is new

steps.detail: endpoint receives provider deliveries, which are at-least-once by design, so two invocations for one event must be assumed
prisma.order.update() writes Order
prisma.webhookEvent.create() writes WebhookEvent
Order is the model being changed
WebhookEvent records the delivery but has no unique field to reject a replay
no transaction, conditional update, or pre-write guard appears anywhere in the handler

findings.explanation: The handler performs 2 separate persisted writes (prisma.order.update, prisma.webhookEvent.create) with no transaction around them and no condition that would make a repeated application a no-op. This endpoint is a provider callback, and callback delivery is at-least-once by design: providers retry on timeout, on a non-2xx response, and sometimes simply twice. Two deliveries of the same event can therefore be in this handler at the same time, on the same or on different instances. Because the writes are independent statements, the two executions interleave freely: both can apply the state change, and the sequence can stop between the first write and the last, leaving the record changed and the rest of the work undone. There is a record kept of the delivery (prisma.webhookEvent.create), but it is written after the state change, so it documents what happened rather than preventing it; and no unique constraint on that store exists to reject a duplicate in any case. No read, conditional update, or upsert guards the first write.
findings.userImpact: A duplicate delivery applies the same change twice. Where the change is a state transition on a payment or an order, the user can be shown a state that was reached by a retry rather than by the event that was actually final — for example a cancelled or failed transaction left showing as completed — and a partial run leaves the record changed with the follow-up work missing. These cases are rare per request and routine at volume, and they tend to surface as support tickets about money rather than as errors in logs.
findings.likelyRootCause: The writes were added in the order the work happens, which reads correctly as a sequence. Nothing in local testing executes the handler twice at once.
downstreamConsequences: Corrupted state persists after the race, so the damage outlives the request that caused it and has to be repaired by hand.
The failure rate rises with traffic and with provider retry storms, which is exactly when there is least capacity to investigate it.
Because each individual request succeeds, no error signal is produced and the problem is invisible to monitoring.
findings.remediation: Make the whole sequence one atomic unit and make a repeat application impossible. Put the writes in a single database transaction so they either all apply or none do. Then add a uniqueness guarantee the database enforces: for a delivery callback, store the provider's event identifier in a table with a unique constraint and insert it inside that same transaction and before the state change, so a duplicate delivery fails the insert and the transaction rolls back untouched. Make the state change conditional as well, so it is a no-op when already applied — for example by including the expected current state in the where clause (a compare-and-set) rather than writing the new state unconditionally. Where several callers legitimately contend for one record, take a row lock (`SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`) or use an optimistic-lock version column and retry on conflict. None of this needs a distributed lock; the database already provides the guarantee.
verificationSteps: Send the same request twice concurrently and confirm exactly one application takes effect and the second is rejected or is a no-op.
Send the same request twice in sequence and confirm the second changes nothing.
Kill the process between the writes (or inject a failure after the first) and confirm no partially applied state remains.
Confirm the uniqueness guarantee is enforced by a database constraint, not only by application code, by attempting the duplicate insert directly.
Add a regression test that runs the handler twice concurrently; this is the test that would have caught it.

findings.title: TypeScript strict mode is switched off in tsconfig.json

evidence.note: strict checking is switched off here

findings.explanation: tsconfig.json sets "strict": false. 13 TypeScript source file(s) are compiled under it. findings.title: Outbound calls in the request path have no timeout (1 call site)

evidence.note: fetch() is awaited in PUT /api/upload with no timeout or abort signal, so the response time of this request is bounded by the upstream, not by us

findings.explanation: An awaited outbound call in a server request handler sets no timeout and no abort signal, and no timeout is configured on the client or anywhere in the enclosing module. How long the request waits is therefore decided by the upstream service. A dependency that fails by returning an error is harmless; a dependency that fails by answering slowly holds one of this application's request slots, one connection, and one set of buffers for as long as it chooses to take. With enough concurrency, all of the slots end up held, and the application stops serving requests that have nothing to do with the slow dependency. How much concurrency that takes depends on the runtime's limits and the real traffic, so this finding needs runtime verification to quantify: what is determinable from the source is that nothing bounds the wait. Note that the platform's default `fetch` has no timeout at all, so the absence of a signal here means the absence of any limit.
findings.userImpact: When an external dependency slows down, users do not get a quick error — they get a page that never finishes loading. Shortly after, parts of the application that do not use that dependency stop responding too, because the slow calls have consumed the capacity to serve anything. From outside it looks like the whole application is down, and it stays that way until the dependency recovers.
findings.likelyRootCause: No timeout is the default in most HTTP clients, so omitting one is easy to do and invisible until a dependency degrades rather than fails.
downstreamConsequences: Held request slots mean one slow dependency takes down endpoints that never call it, which is the standard shape of a cascading failure.
Without a deadline there is nothing for a retry or a circuit breaker to key off, so neither can be added usefully later.
Load balancer and platform timeouts fire first and return a generic error, which hides which dependency was responsible.

With `fetch`, pass `signal: AbortSignal.timeout(ms)`; with a client library, set its timeout option at construction so it applies to every call and cannot be forgotten at a new call site. Choose the value from the budget for the whole request rather than per call, and propagate the remaining budget to calls made further down. Treat the timeout as a real outcome: decide for each call whether to fail the request, serve degraded content, or fall back to a cached value. Where a dependency is not needed to answer the user, move it out of the request path entirely.
verificationSteps: Point each call at a deliberately slow endpoint (a server that accepts the connection and never responds) and confirm the handler returns within the configured deadline.

findings.title: Dockerfile defines no USER, so the container runs as root

evidence.note: no USER directive applies to this stage, so the process keeps the base image default of uid 0 (comments are stripped before matching, so a comment about USER does not count)
this is the process that runs as root

findings.explanation: The runtime stage of Dockerfile contains no USER directive. Official base images do not drop privileges for you, so the application process runs as uid 0 inside the container. A root process inside a container can write anywhere in the image filesystem, install packages at runtime, and bind privileged ports; where the container runtime is not additionally hardened (user namespaces, a seccomp or AppArmor profile, a read-only root filesystem, dropped capabilities) root in the container is a much shorter distance from root on the host than most teams assume. It also makes any code-execution defect elsewhere in the application considerably more useful to an attacker.
findings.userImpact: Users are not affected while the application behaves normally. If an attacker achieves code execution through another defect, running as root is what turns a limited foothold into full control of the container: application files and secrets can be rewritten, a persistent backdoor can be installed, and outbound traffic can be redirected, which users experience as tampered pages, leaked data, or a service that has to be rebuilt from scratch.
findings.likelyRootCause: The Dockerfile was written from a base-image quickstart, which never includes a USER line.
downstreamConsequences: Kubernetes `runAsNonRoot` or a restricted Pod Security Standard will refuse to schedule this image once such a policy is adopted.
Files the container writes to a mounted volume will be owned by root on the host, which is awkward to undo later.
findings.remediation: Create an unprivileged account in the image and switch to it before the process starts: add a group and user (for example `RUN addgroup --system --gid 1001 app && adduser --system --uid 1001 app`, or use the `node` user that Node images already ship), chown only the paths the process must write, then add `USER app` as the last instruction before CMD/ENTRYPOINT. Start the container and confirm it still writes everything it needs (logs, caches, uploads) without permission errors.
Confirm the image still starts under `--read-only` with only the directories it genuinely needs mounted writable.

findings.explanation: src/components/OrderSummary.tsx requests data as part of rendering (fetch at line 21) and renders neither a pending state nor a failure state. There is no pending branch, no error branch, and no catch on the request, so a slow response renders nothing and a failure renders nothing — the same empty output means "working", "empty", and "broken". Two outcomes a user would experience differently are presented identically, with no text for assistive technology to announce. How long the request actually takes was not measured, and the failure path was not executed; those need a running system. This was derived from source only — no browser rendered the page during the scan, so the rendered result was not observed.
findings.userImpact: On a slow connection the user sees an empty region with no indication that anything is happening, so they wait, reload, or leave. When the request fails they see the same empty region, with nothing telling them to retry and no way to distinguish failure from genuinely having no data. A screen-reader user gets no announcement at all, because nothing is rendered to announce.
findings.likelyRootCause: The happy path was built first; the pending and failure paths were left for later because they are not visible in local development against fast, working data.
downstreamConsequences: Support cannot distinguish "no data" from "the request failed" in user reports.
A transient backend failure looks like data loss to the user.
Perceived performance is worse than measured performance, because nothing acknowledges the wait.
findings.remediation: Track the request's three outcomes explicitly — pending, failed, loaded — and render a distinct state for each: a skeleton or spinner inside a role="status" region with aria-live="polite" while pending, a message with a retry action on failure, and a distinct empty state when the request succeeds with no rows. Attach a .catch (or try/catch with await) so a rejection becomes state rather than an unhandled rejection.
verificationSteps: Throttle the network in devtools to "Slow 3G", load the view, and confirm a pending state appears and is announced by a screen reader.
Make the request fail (block the URL in devtools, or stop the backend) and confirm an error message with a retry action is rendered.
Return an empty result and confirm the empty state is distinguishable from both the pending and the failed state.
references: WCAG 2.2 4.1.3 Status Messages (Level AA)
WCAG 2.2 3.3.1 Error Identification (Level A)

findings.title: .github/workflows/deploy.yml pins its pipeline steps by mutable tag rather than commit

evidence.note: `actions/checkout@v4` is referenced by a tag or branch, which the publisher can move to different code at any time
also referenced by a mutable tag

findings.explanation: 2 step reference(s) in this workflow name a tag or branch rather than a commit: actions/checkout@v4, actions/setup-node@v4. A tag is a movable pointer, so the code that runs in the pipeline can change without any change in this repository. These steps execute inside the pipeline with access to its secrets and its checkout, which makes them part of the trust boundary of every release. All of them come from well-known first-party namespaces, which lowers but does not remove the risk.
findings.userImpact: No direct effect in normal operation. If a pipeline step is replaced upstream with hostile code, the consequence for users is a tampered release or stolen deployment credentials, reaching them through the ordinary deployment path and with no local change to point at during the investigation.
findings.likelyRootCause: Tag references are what every example in the marketplace documentation shows.
downstreamConsequences: The pipeline is not reproducible: the same commit can run different step code on different days.
An incident review cannot establish which version of a step ran for a given release.
findings.remediation: Pin each step to a full commit SHA, keeping the tag in a trailing comment for readability, and let an automated update tool raise those SHAs in reviewable pull requests. Give each job the least `permissions:` it needs (start from `contents: read`), avoid exposing secrets to steps that do not need them, and prefer first-party or vendored steps for anything that touches credentials.
verificationSteps: Confirm every `uses:` reference in the workflow is a 40-character commit SHA.
Confirm the pipeline still succeeds after pinning.
Confirm the update tool opens pull requests for new step versions.
references: GitHub — Security hardening for GitHub Actions
OpenSSF Scorecard — Pinned-Dependencies check
OWASP A08:2021 Software and Data Integrity Failures
findings.priorityRationale: P2: low severity with strong confidence, low remediation effort, must wait for 6 prerequisite fix(es).

findings.title: Raw used in a Next.js view instead of the framework's image component

evidence.note: plain element with no srcSet/sizes, so one file is served to every viewport

findings.explanation: This module renders 1 plain element and does not import next/image, so the framework's image pipeline is bypassed: no resizing per viewport, no modern-format negotiation (AVIF/WebP), and no automatic lazy-loading or caching policy. The browser downloads whatever file the src points at, at whatever dimensions it was authored, however small the rendered box is. Explicit width and height are set, which does avoid layout shift. The actual file sizes are not read by this scan, so the size of the waste is unknown.
findings.userImpact: Users download more image data than their screen can use, which is slowest and most expensive exactly where it matters most — mobile connections and metered data. The page also takes longer to become stable and interactive while the images arrive.
findings.likelyRootCause: The markup was written as plain HTML, which works, so the framework component was never swapped in.
downstreamConsequences: Image weight tends to grow silently as content is added, because nothing in the pipeline enforces a ceiling.
Off-screen images compete with above-the-fold content for bandwidth.
findings.remediation: Use next/image (or the framework's equivalent) with explicit width and height, or `fill` with a sized container, so the pipeline generates and caches per-viewport variants in modern formats. Configure the allowed remote patterns narrowly rather than permitting every host. Where a plain must stay — an inline SVG, or an external host that cannot be proxied — declare srcSet and sizes, set width and height, and add loading="lazy" plus decoding="async" for anything below the fold.
verificationSteps: Load the page and record the transferred bytes and the served format for each image before and after the change — that measurement is what confirms the saving.
Confirm the rendered dimensions match the requested variant at mobile, tablet, and desktop widths.
Confirm no layout shift is introduced when the images load.
references: web.dev: Optimize images

findings.title: Dockerfile ships its build toolchain in the runtime image

evidence.note: build-time dependencies are installed into the same stage that produces the runtime image; this file declares only one FROM

findings.explanation: Dockerfile declares a single stage, and that stage installs dependencies without restricting them to production (and in some cases compiles the project) in the same image that is run. Everything needed to build therefore ships to production: compilers, development dependencies, source maps, and the package manager itself. Each of those is extra attack surface that the application never uses at run time, and each contributes to a larger image, which means slower pulls, slower rollbacks, and more to scan and patch.
findings.userImpact: No direct user-visible effect in normal operation. Users feel it during an incident: a larger image takes longer to pull, which lengthens both a deploy and the rollback that ends an outage.
findings.likelyRootCause: A single-stage Dockerfile is the simplest thing that works, and splitting it is rarely urgent.
downstreamConsequences: Vulnerability scanners report findings in build-only packages, which dilutes the signal from ones that matter.
Development dependencies in the runtime image give a code-execution foothold more tools to work with.
findings.remediation: Split the Dockerfile into a build stage and a runtime stage: install all dependencies and build in the first stage, then start the runtime stage from a slim or distroless base and `COPY --from=build` only the build output plus the production dependency tree (installed with `npm ci --omit=dev` or the equivalent). Keep the lockfile copy before the source copy so dependency layers stay cached, and set a non-root USER in the runtime stage.
verificationSteps: Compare `docker image ls` before and after; the runtime image should be substantially smaller.
Run `docker run --rm --entrypoint sh <image> -c 'command -v gcc; ls node_modules/.bin | head'` and confirm build tooling is absent.
Confirm the application still starts and serves a request from the runtime image.
references: Docker — Multi-stage builds
Docker — Best practices for writing Dockerfiles
